[p. 554]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Duha

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿By the morning brightness, and by the night when it is still, your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He detested you.﴾

The meaning of *al-Duha* has already been explained in the previous surah.

It has also been said that what is meant here is the entire day, as in His saying: ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by night while they are asleep? Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them in the morning brightness while they are at play?﴾ [al-A'raf: 97-98]. As for His saying, ﴿and by the night when it is still (*sajā*)﴾, it has been said: it came (*aqbala*); it has been said: its darkness intensified; it has been said: it covered; it has been said: it became calm.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, chose in his dictation the meaning "it became calm."

Ibn Jarir chose that it became calm with its people and settled in its darkness. He said: just as it is said, "a sea that is *sājin*" when it is still. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

*So what is our fault if the sea of your cousin surges, while your sea is still, not concealing the drowned?*

And the saying of the reciter (*rājiz*):

*How wonderful is the moonlit night, and the still night,
and a journey like the cloth of the weaver.*

Al-Qurtubi cited both of these, and he mentioned the saying of Jarir:

*I truly shot you on the day they departed, with eyes
looking out through the gaps of the curtains, still.*

Allah, may He be exalted, swore by the morning brightness and the night here only, because of their suitability to what is sworn about. For they are the two extremes of time and the setting of movement and stillness. He says to him, consoling him: ﴿your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He detested you﴾, neither in night nor in day, as will be detailed later, if Allah wills.

As for His saying, ﴿has not forsaken you﴾, it was read with the doubled letter (*tashdid*), from *tawdi'* (bidding farewell to one who departs). It was also read: "[p. 555] *mā wada'aka*", without doubling, from *al-wad'* (leaving), i.e., from *al-tark* (abandoning), as Abu al-Aswad said:

*I wish I knew about a beloved, what happened
to him in love, until it left him.*

That is, abandoned him. And as another said:

*And there we left the family of 'Amr and 'Amir,
prey for the tips of the spears of thin, dark-brown shafts.*

That is, they left them as prey for the swords.

Abu Hayyan said: *tawdi'* is an intensified form of *wad'*, because one who bids you farewell as one departing has gone to the extreme in leaving you.

The first reading is more well known and more appropriate, because using *wada'a* in the sense of *taraka* (abandoned) is rare.

Al-Qurtubi said, and al-Mubarrad said: they hardly say *wada'a* or *wadhara*, because the *waw* is weak when it is placed first, and they dispensed with it by using *taraka*. What supports al-Mubarrad's view is the dropping of the *waw* in the present tense. You say in the present tense of *wada'a*: *yada'u*, like *yazinu*, *yahibu*, *yarithu*, from *wazana*, *wahaba*, *waritha*. And in the imperative you say: *da'*, *zin*, *hab*. As for *dhar* in the sense of *ut-ruk* (leave), the past tense did not come from it, and the present came as *yadharu*, and the imperative as *dharhum*. Thus the reading of the majority, with doubling, from *wadda'aka* (bidding farewell), is preferred.

We have mentioned this preference because *wada'a* in the sense of *taraka* carries harshness, a kind of estrangement and severance, and this is not fitting for the rank of the Chosen One ﷺ with his Lord. As for *al-muwada'ah* and *al-wada'*, they may occur together with affection and kinship, as they occur between lovers at parting. So even if one bids him farewell in body, one has not bid him farewell in love and tenderness, and in asking about him. This is what fits His saying: ﴿nor has He detested you﴾.

Note:

Here ﴿has not forsaken you﴾ is in the past form, and it is likewise for the future, by the evidence of reality and by the evidence of: ﴿and the Hereafter is better for you than the first﴾ [al-Duha: 4]. For it indicates the continuation of Allah's care for him, until he reaches the Hereafter and finds it better for him than this world. So all of that in between is within the care and protection of his Lord.

It was also reported at the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah that he said to 'Umar: "I am the servant of Allah and His Messenger," i.e., under His mercy and in His protection.

[p. 556] As for His saying, ﴿nor has He detested you﴾, the *kaf* of address was omitted because it is present in what accompanies it, so it indicates it. This is what the commentators said.

Some of them said: it was left out for the sake of the verse-ending (*ra's al-ayah*). What appears from the subtle address, the tender intimacy, and the gentle approaches, is that bidding farewell indicates loyalty and affection, so the *kaf* of address was made explicit in it, i.e., your farewell could not be made to you, though you are the beloved and the Chosen One, the one brought near.

As for *qala* (detested): it carries the meaning of hatred, so it was not suitable to make it explicit, out of exceeding care to keep his ﷺ intention far from anything of this meaning, just as you say to one dear to you: "I have honored you and did not humiliate you; I have brought you near and did not push you away," out of dislike of uttering his humiliation or hatred, or declaring it concerning him.

*Al-qala*: it is pronounced with a long or short vowel; it is *al-bughd* (hatred). It is with a long vowel when you open the *qaf*, and short when you vowel it with a *kasra*. It may be from the *waw* root or the *ya'* root. Al-Qurtubi mentioned: Tha'lab recited:

*The days of Umm al-Ghamr, we have not hated them,
and had you willed, I would have kissed her eyes.*

And Kuthayyir 'Azzah said:

*Treat us badly or well, there is no blame on her with us,
nor one who is hated if she turns away.*

The first said: *fa-qalaha* from the *waw* root, and the second said: *maqliyyah* from the *ya'* root, and both are evidence in the language.

What supports this meaning in the biography (*sirah*) and confirms the continuing friendship of Allah, may He be glorified, with His beloved, His care for him, and His protection of him, is that when his uncle wept over him, his uncle said concerning that:

*By Allah, they will not reach you with their assembly
until I am laid in the dust, buried.*

Ibn Hisham mentioned concerning his uncle's care for him: when night fell and they wanted to sleep, he left him to sleep with his children. When each had taken his bed, his uncle deliberately took one of his sons, made him stand, and brought Muhammad ﷺ to sleep in his place, and took his son to sleep in Muhammad's place ﷺ. If someone intending harm came, he would see his place at the beginning of the night, and when the one who intended evil came, the harm fell upon his son, and Muhammad ﷺ was safe. Likewise did al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) on the departure for the Hijrah, on their way to the cave. He (may Allah be pleased with him) sometimes walked in front of him ﷺ and sometimes walked behind him. He ﷺ asked him about [p. 557] that, and he said: "I remember the pursuer ahead, so I walk in front of you, and I remember the pursuit, so I walk behind you." He ﷺ said: "Would you like it if harm came upon you, O Abu Bakr?" He said: "Yes, may my father and mother be your ransom, O Messenger of Allah." Then he said: "If I perish, I perish alone; and if you perish, the message perishes with you." That was his uncle in the days of ignorance, not upon his religion ﷺ; and this was Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him).

**The Words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first life﴾**

"Khayr" (خَيْرٌ) comes as a verbal noun (maṣdar), as in His saying: ﴿if he leaves behind wealth﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 180], meaning: much wealth. It also comes as an elative (ʾafʿal al-tafḍīl, the comparative/superlative form) with the hamza dropped. Here it is an elative, as shown by the mention of the counterpart and by the particle "min" (from/than). This indicates that He, glorified is He, gave him many good things in this world, but what he will have in the Hereafter is better and superior to what He gave him in this world. It may give the impression that the Hereafter is better for him ﷺ alone than the first life, but the text indicates that it is better for the righteous (al-abrār) all together, as in His saying: ﴿And what is with Allah is better for the righteous﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 198].

The Shaykh, may God's mercy be upon us and upon him, has already explained that the goodness for the righteous is with Allah, that is, on the Day of Resurrection, through what He has prepared for them, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾ [Al-Infiṭār: 13], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor﴾ [Al-Insān: 5].

As for the explanation of the goodness here regarding the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, it is the explanation of the good in this world first, then the explanation of what is superior to it in the Hereafter.

As for this world, indicated by the elative, that is, because it indicates that the two matters share the attribute while one exceeds the other, He has pointed to it in this surah and in the one after it. In this surah is His saying: ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾ [Al-Ḍuḥā: 6], meaning: from his birth and upbringing. Allah, glorified is He, took care of him from his childhood, protected him from the defilement of shirk, purified him, opened his chest, and cleansed him. Despite his orphanhood, he was the master of the youth of Quraysh, as his uncle said when proposing to Khadījah for his marriage to her: "A young man whom no young man of Quraysh can equal in forbearance, intellect and character, except that he outweighs him."

And His saying: ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ ﴿And He found you poor and made you self-sufficient﴾ [Al-Ḍuḥā: 7–8].

All of this, as will be explained, consists of blessings which He enumerates for him. They are among the greatest good things of this world (p-558), from his childhood to his youth and old age, then his being chosen for the message, then his being protected from the people, then his being given victory over the enemies, the manifestation of his religion, and the exaltation of His word.

On the immaterial side is what comes in the surah after it: ﴿Did We not expand for you your chest?﴾ ﴿And We relieved you of your burden﴾ ﴿Which had weighed upon your back﴾ ﴿And We raised high for you your remembrance﴾ [Al-Sharḥ: 1–4].

As for the superiority of the Hereafter over the first life, it is in accordance with His saying: ﴿And your Lord is going to give you, and you will be satisfied﴾ [Al-Ḍuḥā: 5]. And there is no request after satisfaction. In summary: the first life is a abode of action, obligation and struggle, while the Hereafter is an abode of recompense, reward and honor. So it is, without doubt, better than the first life.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 93, verse 5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be content﴾

It is emphasized with the lam (al-lam, the emphatic particle) and with "sawfa" (the future particle). Some scholars said: He will give him in this world, through the completion of the religion, the elevation of the word of Allah, and victory over the enemies.

The majority (al-jumhur) hold that it refers to the Hereafter. Although this is in general terms (ijmal), it has been detailed in some places, the greatest of which is what His saying, exalted is He, points to: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾ [al-Isra': 79].

The Sunnah has explained the praised station (al-maqam al-mahmud), which is the station that the first and the last will envy him for, as in the hadith of the Great Intercession (al-shafa'ah al-uzma), when every prophet withdraws and says: "Myself, myself," until they come to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he says: "I am for it, I am for it." etc.

Among them is the Hawd al-Mawrud (the Pool of Abundance), and what his Ummah was distinguished with, [coming forth] radiant with white marks, coming to the Pool.

Among them is al-Wasilah (the means, the intermediate station), which is a high, lofty station that is fitting only for one servant, as in the hadith: "When you hear the muezzin, say the same as he says, then send blessings upon me, and ask Allah for me al-Wasilah, for it is a station in Paradise that is fitting only for one servant, and I hope that I will be he."

If it is for only one servant, then who will vie for it? When he hoped that his Lord would make it his, he asked the Ummah to ask for it for him. This is among what confirms that it is his, for otherwise he would not have asked for it, nor hoped for it, nor commanded that it be requested for him. Without doubt, he is more deserving of it than all of creation, since the best of creation are the Messengers, and he (ﷺ) precedes them in this world, just as in the Isra' he preceded them in prayer in Bayt al-Maqdis.

(p-559) Among them is the intercession for entry into Paradise, as in the hadith: "He (ﷺ) is the first for whom Paradise will be opened, and Ridwan, the keeper of Paradise, will say to him: 'I have been commanded not to open it for anyone before you.'"

Among them is the multiple intercession, until no one of his Ummah remains in the Fire, as in the hadith: "I will not be content while one of my Ummah is in the Fire." We ask Allah to grant us his intercession and to bring us to his Pool. Amin.

His special intercession for a particular person is for his uncle Abu Talib, by which his punishment is lightened for him.

Among them is his testimony over the Messengers, and the testimony of his Ummah over the nations, and other things. These are without doubt gifts from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise, to His beloved and chosen, the noble one, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, and upon his family and companions, with abundant peace.

Note (tanbih).

The lam in "wa-la-l-akhirah" and in "wa-la-sawfa" is for emphasis, not for oath (qasam). In the first, it entered upon the subject (mubtada'); in the second, the subject is omitted, its estimated form being: "la-anta sawfa yu'tika rabbuka fa-tarda." So said Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 93, verse 6:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾

The meaning of "orphan" (yatim) was explained earlier, at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive﴾ [al-Insan: 8].

The Messenger ﷺ lost his father while he was still in the womb, six months old, and his mother died while returning from Madinah, at Al-Abwa', when he ﷺ was [a child].

It has been said that his orphanhood was because no one has a right over him, as related by Abu Hayyan.

What appears to be the case is that his orphanhood relates to His saying: ﴿Your Lord has not forsaken you﴾, meaning that Allah, exalted is He, would take charge of his affairs from his childhood. The meaning of Allah's sheltering him was explained earlier. So his orphanhood was for the sake of displaying His favour, because the orphan of yesterday became the master of tomorrow and the guardian of orphans.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 93, verse 7:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾. Ḍalāl (going astray) occurs in both the sensory and the figurative sense. The first is like one who wanders lost on a road he is travelling; the second is like one who abandons the truth and does not follow it.

Some scholars said: the intended meaning here is the first, as though he had strayed into one of the valleys of Makkah, or on his way to al-Shām, and the like.

Others said: it is merely an expression for his not having been taught at first, and then his being granted knowledge of what he did not know, as in His saying: ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was; but We made it a light, guiding by it whomever We will of Our servants﴾ [al-Shūrā: 52].

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, had previously discussed this matter in several places:

First: in Surat Yūsuf, at His saying: ﴿Indeed, our father is in clear error﴾ [Yūsuf: 8], where he cited the linguistic evidences for ḍalāl there.

Second: in Surat al-Kahf, at His saying: ﴿those whose effort is lost in the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf: 104].

Third: in Surat al-Shu'arā', at His saying: ﴿He said, "I did it then, while I was of those astray"﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 20].

And also in removing the appearance of inconsistency. All of this suffices as a substitute for any other discussion.

Among the curious things is what Abū Ḥayyān mentioned at this verse, where he said: "I saw in a dream that I was reflecting on this sentence, and I immediately said: '[He found you] wa-wajadaka': that is, He found your people lost, and guided them through you. Then I said: it is by omitting a noun (muḍāf), like: '[And ask the town]' [Yūsuf: 82]." End of quote.

al-Naysābūrī also cited this as one interpretation of the verse.

On this occasion I will mention two dreams I had, which I had not intended to mention until I saw this of Abū Ḥayyān, so I took comfort in it in mentioning them. They are: The first: when I reached Surat Nūn, at His saying: ﴿And indeed you are of a great character﴾ [al-Qalam: 4]. Among the methodology of Adwā' al-Bayān is interpreting the Qur'an by the Qur'an, and this is a general description, and the ḥadīth of 'Ā'ishah: "His character was the Qur'an." So I began to think about how to elaborate this meaning from the Qur'an, and to explain its judgment, his forgiveness, his patience, his generosity, his kindness, his compassion, his mercy, (p-561) his gentleness, his jihad and his worship. All of this made me stand bewildered, and I paused from writing for several days. Then I saw the Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, in a dream, as though we were at the Islamic University in al-Madīnah al-Munawwarah, and as though he were not in his usual vigor. I asked him: "What do you have today?"

He said: "I have a tafsīr." I said: "Are you teaching today?" He said: "No." I said: "What is this in your hand?" – a notebook in his hand – He said: "A tafsīr notebook," that is, the one he was going to explain – and it was a manuscript. I said to him: "From where in the Qur'an?" He said: "From the beginning of Nūn to the end of the Qur'an." I was eager to take it so that I could copy from it, but I did not dare to ask for it openly. Instead I said to him: "Since you are not teaching today, give it to me, and I will clean it up and bind it for you, and bring it to you tomorrow." He gave it to me, and I woke up joyful and began writing.

The second time was in Surat al-Muṭaffifīn. When I wrote on the meaning of tatfīf (short-measure), then I reflected on the severe threat against it together with what might occur in it of a small amount, until I reflected that it has a connection with ribā, if one kind is sold for the same kind with a difference in measure and excess occurs. But I did not find anyone who had said this. Then I saw, as the sleeper sees, that I was with the Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, but he did not speak with me about anything of tafsīr.

After he went away from me, suddenly a person I did not know said, while I was listening, without addressing the speech to me: "Indeed, in short-measure there is ribā, if iron is sold for iron," and another word of similar meaning, which I forgot after I awoke.

I have mentioned this in emulation of Abū Ḥayyān, because I find in it comfort. I ask Allah to grant us success in what He loves and is pleased with, to guide us to the right path, and to fulfil the good tidings contained in the dream. And success is from Allah, Exalted.

The author said in (Dafʿ Īhām al-Iḍṭirāb ʿan Āyāt al-Kitāb):

(p-454) In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Sūrat al-Ḍuḥā

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾.

The apparent meaning of this noble verse gives the impression that the Prophet (ﷺ) was astray before revelation, although His saying: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth, the natural disposition (fiṭrah) of Allah upon which He created mankind﴾ [al-Rūm: 30] indicates that he (ﷺ) was created upon this upright religion. It is known that his parents did not make him a Jew, nor a Christian, nor a Magian; rather he remained upon the fiṭrah until Allah sent him as a Messenger. What supports this is what is established: that the first revelation came while he was worshipping in the cave of Ḥirā'. That worship before the revelation is evidence of his remaining upon the fiṭrah.

The answer is that the meaning of His saying: ﴿lost and guided﴾ is: unaware of what you now know of the laws and the secrets of the sciences of religion, which are not known by natural disposition nor by reason, but are known only by revelation. So He guided you to that through what He revealed to you. Thus the meaning of ḍalāl according to this view is departure from knowledge.

From this meaning is His saying: ﴿lest one of them err, and the other remind her﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282].

And His saying: ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 52]; and His saying: ﴿They said, "By Allah, you are in your old error"﴾ [Yūsuf: 95]; and the poet's saying:

"And Salmā thinks that I seek another in place of her; I see her wandering in error."

What supports this is His saying: ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was﴾ [al-Shūrā: 52], because faith here means the laws of the religion of Islam.

And His saying: ﴿And indeed you were before it among the unaware﴾ [Yūsuf: 3]; and His saying: ﴿and taught you what you did not know﴾ (p-455) [al-Nisā': 113]; and His saying: ﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be bestowed upon you, except as a mercy from your Lord﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 86].

It has been said that what is meant by His saying "lost" is his wandering as a child in the valleys of Makkah. It has also been said: his wandering during his journey to al-Shām. The first view is the correct one, and Allah knows best, and attributing knowledge to Allah is safest.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 93, verse 8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He found you poor and made you rich﴾.

Al-'a'il (العائل) means the one who has dependents (ṣāḥib al-ʿiyāl), and it was said that al-'a'il is the poor man, on the basis that need is a necessary consequence of having dependents, though it is not necessarily so. The contrast of "'a'il" with "aghnā" (made rich) indicates that the meaning of "'a'il" is "poor" (faqīran). For this reason the poet said:

"The poor man does not know when his riches will come, and the rich man does not know when he will become poor."

"And you do not know, though you urge a young camel calf, whether it will belong to another or whether the weaned young camel will be yours."

(p-562) This is among the blessings which Allah mentions to His Prophet ﷺ in enumerating the favours upon him, and that He did not abandon him nor forsake him. He was indeed poor in wealth, and Allah made him rich through the wealth of his uncle.

His uncle said in the sermon of his marriage to Khadijah: "If he is poor in wealth, whatever dowry you wish will be upon me." Then Allah made him rich through the wealth of Khadijah, when she placed her wealth under his control.

Al-Naysaburi said, and his words are: It is narrated that "he ﷺ entered upon Khadijah while he was distressed, and she said: What is the matter with you? He said: 'The times are times of drought; if I spend the wealth, your wealth will be depleted, and I would be ashamed before you; and if I do not spend, I fear Allah.'" So she invited the Quraysh, among whom was al-Siddiq. Al-Siddiq said: She brought out dinars and placed them until they reached an amount I had never seen before, and she said: "Bear witness that this wealth is his; if he wishes he may distribute it, and if he wishes he may keep it."

This story, although its chain is not mentioned, is not strange for Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her, to do this for him ﷺ, and she had already done something greater than this, when she entered the Shi'b with him, leaving her wealth and choosing to share with him ﷺ in the hardship of his life, until they ate the leaves of trees, while her wealth was abundant in her house.

Then came the Hijrah and the support of the Ansar. He came to Madinah leaving his wealth and the wealth of Khadijah, to the extent that al-Siddiq paid the price of the enclosure for building the Mosque. After that came the spoils of Banu al-Nadir, and he would pass a month, then another month, then another month, without fire being kindled in his house; rather, they were the two blacks: dates and water.

Then came the spoils of Hunayn, and he gave the gift of one who does not fear poverty, and he returned with nothing. The wealth of Bahrain came, and al-'Abbas took what he could carry. Finally, he ﷺ died while his armour was pawned for thirty sa' of barley.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He found you poor and made you rich﴾ points to this situation, because "aghnā" (made rich) is an expression by a verb, and it indicates renewal and occurrence. He ﷺ was, in terms of wealth, in a state after state. But the reality is that his ﷺ richness was before everything: it was the richness of the self and independence from people, and it suffices that he ﷺ was the most generous of people.

When Jibril met him and studied the Qur'an with him, he was like the sent wind. So he ﷺ was the exemplar (p-563) in both states, in the state of poverty and the state of wealth: if his wealth was little he was patient, and if it increased he gave and gave thanks.

"Be independent, as your Lord has made you independent through richness; and if poverty befalls you, then adorn yourself [with patience]."

Among what shows the greatness of Allah's gift to him is what surpasses every gift: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated and the magnificent Qur'an﴾ [al-Hijr: 87], then He said: ﴿Do not extend your eyes toward what We have given to pairs of them, and do not grieve over them, and lower your wing to the believers﴾ [al-Hijr: 88].

They differed concerning the comparison between the patient poor man and the grateful rich man, but Allah, exalted is He, combined for His Messenger ﷺ both matters, in order to outline the perfect exemplar in both states.

Note.

In the verse there is an indication that sheltering, guidance and richness are from Allah, since they are attributed here to Allah, exalted is He.

But in the context there is a subtle point, which is the manner of affirmation: He brings the particle of address (the kāf of address): "Did He not find you an orphan? Did He not find you astray? Did He not find you poor?" to emphasise the affirmation. Orphanhood, misguidance and poverty were not attributed to Allah, although all of it is from Allah. It is He who placed orphanhood upon him, and it is He, glorified is He, from whom it comes whenever He found him in it; that is because of the pain it causes him. So He did not explicitly attribute it to Allah, and because of the affirmation upon him, He made the pronoun of address prominent.

As for the enumeration of blessings: "So He sheltered [you], guided [you], and made [you] rich," all of it is attributed to the pronoun of the Benefactor, and He did not make the pronoun of address prominent.

The exegetes said: this is for the sake of observing the ends of verses and the rhyme. But what appears, and Allah knows best, is that since there is a favour in it, and these are material blessings, He did not make the pronoun prominent, lest the obligation weigh heavily upon him; whereas He made it prominent in: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ ﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾ [al-Sharh: 1–2], ﴿And We raised for you your mention﴾ [al-Sharh: 4], because these are spiritual blessings, in which He alone is singular. ﷺ. And Allah knows best.

[p. 564] The Almighty's words: ﴿So as for the orphan, do not oppress him﴾ ﴿and as for the one who asks, do not repel him﴾ ﴿and as for the blessing of your Lord, proclaim it﴾.

The use of the particle *fa* (so/then) here implies either a sequence (*tafri'*, a logical consequence), which is weak, or an explicit enumeration of several matters. Some have explained the sentences as if preceded by "*mahma yakun min shay'*" (whatever may be the case).

Here the Almighty presents three matters. The first is the treatment of orphans, as He says: ﴿So as for the orphan, do not oppress him﴾, meaning: just as Allah sheltered you, shelter him, and just as He honoured you, honour him.

They said: *qahr* (oppression) of the orphan is taking his property and wronging him.

It was also said that it was read with a *kaf*, *takhhar* (to be harsh), and they said it has the same meaning as *qahr* but is stronger.

It was also said that it means a frowning countenance, and the meaning is more general, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from anxiety and grief, from incapacity and laziness, from cowardice and miserliness, from being overcome by debt and from the oppression of men." So *qahr* is more general than all of that.

Considering the numerous Qur'anic texts concerning the orphan, which exceed twenty passages, they can be classified into five categories, all revolving around warding off harms from him and bringing benefits to him, in his property and in his person. Four of these concern his property and person, and the fifth concerns his marital status. As for warding off harm from him in his property, it is in the Almighty's words: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner﴾. It occurs twice in the surah *al-An'am* and once in the surah *al-Isra'* [al-Isra' 34]. In each of the two surahs it is within the ten well-known injunctions in *al-An'am*, beginning with His words: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite to you what your Lord has forbidden you: that you associate nothing with Him, and be good to your parents﴾ [al-An'am 151].

He mentions the killing of children, approaching immoralities, killing a soul, and then the property of the orphan: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner﴾.

It is noted that the prohibition is directed at merely approaching his property, except in the best manner. The Almighty has explained "the best manner" in His words: ﴿Whoever is wealthy let him abstain, and whoever is poor let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾ [al-Nisa' 6].

The jurists have stated that whoever manages the property of an orphan and deserves a wage, he is entitled to the lesser of two things: either his maintenance (*nafaqah*) in his own person, or his wage for his work. That is, if the work deserves a wage of a thousand *riyals*, and his maintenance requires five hundred, he takes only his maintenance; and if the work deserves a wage of a hundred *riyals*, and his maintenance is five hundred, he takes only his wage, a hundred, in order to preserve the property.

Then, after this prohibition against approaching the orphan's property, some souls may aspire to small differences by way of trickery or the like, such as substituting one thing for another, which becomes a way to exchange good for bad. Hence the Almighty's words came: ﴿And give the orphans their property, and do not substitute the bad for the good, and do not devour their property along with your own property. Indeed, that is a great sin﴾ [al-Nisa' 2].

*Hub* (sin) is the greatest of sins. In it is the prohibition against substituting the good of his property with the bad property of the guardian or of others, out of envy for his property. Just as He forbade mixing his property with the property of others as a means of consuming it together with the property of others. This is a prohibition against trickery and a blocking of the means (*sadd al-dhari'ah*), in order to preserve his property.

Then comes the severe threat in a frightening form in the Almighty's words: ﴿Indeed, those who devour the property of orphans unjustly only consume fire into their bellies, and they will burn in a blaze﴾ [al-Nisa' 10].

* *

The scholars have agreed that the verse includes, in the prohibition against consuming the property of orphans, everything that involves destruction or loss, whether by actual eating, or by embezzlement, or by burning, or by drowning. This is what is known among the scholars of *usul* (legal theory) as *al-ilhaq bi-nafy al-fari* (assimilation by negating any distinction), since there is no difference for the orphan in the loss of his property, whether it is through eating, or burning with fire, or drowning in water, or even through negligence in it. It is all a loss to him, and all of this is for preserving his property.

Finally, when the preservation of his property is achieved, one does not approach it except in the best manner, does not exchange it for something lesser, does not mix it with one's own property in order to consume it, and does not transgress against it by any destruction; it remains preserved for him until his orphanhood ends and his maturity is established. Then comes the Almighty's words: ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age; then if you perceive in them maturity of judgment, release to them their property, and do not consume it extravagantly or hastily, fearing that they will grow up﴾ [al-Nisa' 6].

Then He surrounded the handing over of the property to him with the requirements of preservation, in His words at the end of the verse: ﴿So when you release to them their property, then have witnesses over them﴾ [al-Nisa' 6], that is, so that there will be no dispute afterwards.

At the end, Allah reminds those who are restrained by the awareness of Allah with His words: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner﴾ [al-Nisa' 6]. In it is an indication that his property is handed over to him after a precise accounting of what is his and what is owed by him.

And whatever the precision of the reckoning, Allah will call them to account for it: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner﴾. All of this concerns the preservation of his property.

As for bringing benefits, we find, first, that He placed him alongside parents and relatives in several places, among them the Almighty's words: ﴿Say: Whatever wealth you spend should go to parents and relatives and orphans﴾ [al-Baqarah 215].

Among them is His mention of him among the kinds of righteousness, namely belief in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book and the prophets, and giving wealth out of love for it to relatives, orphans, and the needy﴾ [al-Baqarah 177], to the end of the verse.

Among them is what was introduced into the subject, where a share in the inheritance was assigned to him in the Almighty's words: ﴿And when the division takes place, if relatives, orphans and the needy are present, provide for them from it﴾ [al-Nisa' 8], apart from the discussions of the verse from other aspects. And once more He assigns them a share in what is of higher rank, in His words: ﴿And know that whatever you acquire of spoils, a fifth of it belongs to Allah and to the Messenger and to the near relatives and the orphans and the needy and the traveller, if you have believed in Allah﴾ [al-Anfal 41].

Likewise in the surah *al-Hashr*, in His words: ﴿What Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah and to the Messenger and to the near relatives and the orphans and the needy and the traveller﴾ [al-Hashr 7], to the end of the verse.

Thus Allah placed them alongside the near relatives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

He also placed the orphan within the general description of the righteous, and as a means of reaching the highest ranks of bliss, in His words: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor﴾ [al-Insan 5].

He mentioned their deeds, among which: "that they ﴿fulfil their vows﴾" [al-Insan 7], and after that, that they: ﴿give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive﴾ [al-Insan 8].

And He made this feeding the crossing of the steep path, in His words: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path. And what can make you know what is the steep path? It is freeing a neck, or feeding on a day of severe hunger, an orphan of near relationship, or a needy man in misery﴾ [al-Balad 11-15], to the end of the verse.

And indeed we find something greater than that: that Allah brought al-Khidr and Musa, peace be upon them, to set up a wall for two orphans, over a treasure belonging to them, until they reach maturity, in His words: ﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure for them, and their father had been righteous. So your Lord intended that they reach their maturity and extract their treasure as a mercy from your Lord. And I did not do it of my own accord﴾ [al-Kahf 82].

[p. 567] This is the financial aspect of warding off harm from him in preserving his property, and from the aspect of bringing benefit to him through wealth.

As for the psychological aspect, it is as follows:

First: not causing him distress in his soul. Among it is the Almighty's words: ﴿Have you seen the one who denies the Recompense? That is the one who repulses the orphan, and does not urge the feeding of the needy﴾ [al-Ma'un 1-3].

And among it His words: ﴿No! Rather, you do not honour the orphan, nor do you urge one another to feed the needy﴾ [al-Fajr 17-18], where He mentioned honouring him first, as an indication of it.

Second: in kindness towards him. Among it is the Almighty's words: ﴿Worship none but Allah, and be good to parents and to near relatives and orphans﴾ [al-Baqarah 83], so he is treated kindly just as one treats kindly one's parents and relatives.

Among it is a question and its answer from Allah, the Exalted: ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Setting right their affairs is good. And if you mix with them, they are your brothers. And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾ [al-Baqarah 220], that is, you deal with them as you deal with brothers, and this is the highest degree of kindness and goodness; therefore He said: ﴿And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾.

In mentioning the corrupter before the reformer there is an indication of the severity of the warning against corruption in dealing with him, and because it is the place of warning. In another passage He placed them in the position of children, in His words: ﴿And let those fear who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them; so let them fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice﴾ [al-Nisa' 9].

That is, even in addressing them, since they are in the position of their own children. Indeed, perhaps they will have children later who will be orphans after them. Just as they fear for their children if they become orphans after them, so let them treat well the orphans in their charge. This is the utmost degree of care and attention.

These are the texts of the Qur'an on the good treatment of the orphan and not harming him, which elaborate the general statement of His words: ﴿So as for the orphan, do not oppress him﴾ [al-Duha 9].

Neither with an unsuitable word, nor by depriving him of something he needs, nor by destroying his property, nor by trickery to consume and waste it, nor by anything at all, whether in his person or in his property.

[p. 568] The hadiths from the Sunnah on this are numerous and reach the utmost extent in his regard. The Prophet (ﷺ) was the most merciful of people towards him and the most compassionate to him, to the extent that he said: "I and the one who sponsors an orphan will be in Paradise like these two," pointing to the index finger and the middle finger, and separating them. Narrated by al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi.

In the narration of Abu Hurayrah in Muslim and Malik: "The one who sponsors an orphan, whether his own or someone else's." That is, a relative of his or a stranger to him.

In Ahmad and al-Tabarani, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever takes in an orphan from among two Muslim parents, and feeds him and gives him drink, Paradise becomes due for him." Al-Mundhiri said: the narrators of Ahmad are reliable (*muhtajj bihim*) except 'Ali ibn Zayd.

In Ibn Majah, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The best house among the Muslims is a house in which there is an orphan who is treated well. And the worst house among the Muslims is a house in which there is an orphan who is mistreated."

And in Abu Dawud there is something even further than this and that, to the extent that a mother neglects her own interests for the sake of her orphans, in the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I and a woman with a blackened (*saf'a*) cheek, like these two on the Day of Resurrection," and Yazid ibn Zuray' (with a *fatha* on the *zay* and a sukun on the *ya*) gestured with his hand, with the middle finger and the index finger: "a woman who has become a widow (*amat zawjaha*), who has become a widow (*ayyim*) by the death of her husband, possessed of position and beauty, who has confined herself to her orphans until they are gone or have died."

Allah also made it a remedy for hardness of heart, as Ahmad narrated, and its narrators are the narrators of the authentic collections: from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that "a man complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of the hardness of his heart, so he said: 'Stroke the head of the orphan, and feed the needy.'"

Here a subtle secret is revealed in the ideal character of Islamic legislation, in that Allah, the Exalted, addresses the best and most merciful of creation, the most compassionate and gentle towards the servants of Allah, who is described by the Almighty's words: ﴿To the believers he is kind and merciful﴾ [al-Tawbah 128], and His words: ﴿And indeed, you are of a great moral character﴾ [al-Qalam 4], so that he would be an ideal example for a nation whose hearts had grown hard and whose natures had become coarse, so they show no mercy to the weak and render no right except by strength; they adhere to the principle: whoever is mighty plunders, and whoever prevails seizes. They boast of injustice and disparage trustworthiness, as their poet said:

A tribe that does not break a covenant of protection, and does not wrong people by the weight of a mustard seed.

And their sage says:

Whoever does not defend his watering place with his weapon will be destroyed, and whoever does not wrong people will not be wronged.

Pre-Islamic peoples used to bury their daughters alive, and they deprived women of their share of inheritance. ﴿And you devour the inheritance, devouring it all greedily﴾, ﴿and you love wealth with an intense love﴾. He (Allah) turned their standards upside down and corrected their understanding. He softened their hearts and refined their dispositions, so they became gentle toward this weak one and preserved his right.

The reality of this wise divine legislation, for fourteen centuries, surpasses everything that the hopes of all human civilizations aspire to. It achieves the perfection of social solidarity (al-takaful al-ijtima'i) in its most splendid meanings, which is alluded to in the noble verse: ﴿And let those fear [Allah] who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would fear for them. So let them fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice﴾ [al-Nisa': 9]. Thus He made the one who sponsors an orphan today, in effect, acting also for the future, as if he were to leave weak offspring behind. Here He expressed the orphans by what necessarily accompanies them, namely weakness, to highlight the orphan's need for kindness because of his weakness. Those (who are tempted to mistreat orphans) will thus be the object of their own fear for them, because of their weakness. So let them treat the orphans under their care as they would like others to treat their orphans after them.

In this way the verse sets before us a social solidarity in the sponsorship of the orphan. Indeed, the orphan himself is the orphan of today and the man of tomorrow. As you treat him well, he will treat your orphans well after you. And as you deal with others, so you will be dealt with. If it is good, the good is repaid with good, and the one who initiates is more noble. If it is evil, it is repaid with its like, and the one who initiates is more unjust.

Along with this reciprocal right, Islam urges it, cares for it, encourages kindness toward the orphan and rewards it abundantly, warns against harming him, and imposes severe punishment for it.

What we have presented may be somewhat lengthy, but it is a fulfillment of the orphan's right first, and an expression of how much the orphan suffers second.

Note.

Disciplining the orphan and being firm with him is not a form of harming him; rather, it is for his benefit, as it was said:

*He was harsh so that they would be restrained, and whoever is wise, let him be harsh at times toward one who is merciful.*

And His saying: ﴿As for the one who asks, do not turn him away﴾. They said: the one who asks (al-sa'il) is the poor and needy person who asks for what will meet his need. This is the counterpart of His saying: ﴿And He found you poor and made you self-sufficient﴾, meaning: just as Allah made you self-sufficient, and without your asking, so when a questioner comes to you, do not rebuke him, even if you must return an answer in the manner that is best.

It is known that a gentle reply may take the place of giving in responding to the one who asks. When the Prophet (ﷺ) did not have anything to give the questioner, he would promise him a good promise of a time of ease, taking this from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle word﴾ [al-Isra: 28].

Al-Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, cited two verses at this verse on this meaning, which are the saying of the poet:

"If there is no silver one day that I can give to the askers, then I am a supple stick (layyin al-'ud)."

"The askers will not lose good from my character: either my giving, or a good refusal."

So let speech bring happiness if wealth does not bring happiness.

It was also said: the one who asks is the one who seeks clarification on matters of religion and the one who seeks guidance. They said this is the counterpart of His saying: ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾, meaning: do not rebuke the one who seeks sufficiency or the one who seeks guidance, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ ﴿because the blind man came to him﴾ [Abasa: 1-2].

The Prophet (ﷺ) was merciful and compassionate toward the ignorant until he learned, as in the story of the Bedouin who urinated in the mosque when the Companions shouted at him. He said to them: "Do not interrupt him." Then the Bedouin said: "O Allah, have mercy on me and on Muhammad, and have mercy on no one else with us ever." Similarly was the other man who came striking his chest and tearing his hair, saying: "I am ruined and have ruined others; I had intercourse with my wife in Ramadan." Until it came to pass that he gave him a basket (faraq) of food, by which he might atone for his sin. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, is there anyone poorer than us?" He said: "Go and feed it to your family."

The Prophet (ﷺ) would stop for a woman on the road and listen to her until those with him became impatient, yet he would bear with her and not rebuke her, but would answer her questions.

The Prophet (ﷺ) also urged honoring the seeker of knowledge, and explained that the angels lower their wings for the seeker of knowledge, and that the fish in the sea seek forgiveness for him, out of pleasure at what he does.

And His saying: ﴿But as for the blessing of your Lord, proclaim it﴾. "Blessing" (ni'mah) is everything Allah bestows upon the servant, and it is everything the servant enjoys of wealth, well-being, guidance, and support, derived from ease (nu'umah) and gentleness (layn). It has been said that what is meant by it is the things mentioned, and proclaiming them is giving thanks for them in practice: sheltering the orphan as Allah sheltered you, giving to the beggar as Allah enriched you, and teaching the seeker of guidance as Allah taught you. This is part of giving thanks for the blessing, meaning: just as Allah has bestowed blessings upon you, you should bestow blessings upon others, emulating Allah's action toward you.

It has also been said that proclaiming the blessing of Allah is conveying from Allah, from the verses and the hadith. Here the word "blessing" is general, because it is indefinite and in the construct form, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾ [an-Nahl: 53], meaning every blessing. However, what appears to me is that it refers most clearly to revelation, or it is most fitting for it, or it is the greatest of them, because of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion, and completed My blessing upon you, and have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], where He said "My blessing," while here it is "the blessing of your Lord." In my view, it is not far-fetched that the Prophet (ﷺ) sacrificed one hundred camels at the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajj al-Wada'), when Allah revealed this verse to him, and he did so in gratitude to Allah for the completion of the blessing through the perfecting of the religion.

The commentators have said concerning the connection of this surah with what precedes it: the one before it concerns Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, ﴿And the most righteous will be spared it﴾, ﴿who gives his wealth to purify himself﴾, ﴿and no one has a blessing with him that must be repaid﴾, ﴿except seeking the countenance of his Lord, the Most High﴾, ﴿and he will surely be satisfied﴾ [al-Layl: 17–21]. Here, concerning the Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He detested you﴾, ﴿and the Hereafter is better for you than the first﴾, ﴿and your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied﴾ [ad-Duha: 3–5], with the great difference in the giving and in the address.

The reality is that the connections between short surahs are clearer than the connections between verses within a single surah, as between these two surahs: "by the night" with "by the morning brightness." Then between "by the morning brightness" and "Did We not expand for you your breast," it is the completion of the blessings which Allah, Exalted is He, enumerates upon His Messenger. And so it is, as will be pointed out in its place, Allah willing.

I know with certainty that some scholars did not take these connections into account. However, where the connection is clear, it should not be neglected, and where it is hidden, one should not strain to find it.
